head: Samsung set fire
to its own phones.
slides.sub: Why burning 150,000 devices saved a brand.

image.label: A pile of mobile phones burning in a factory yard
image.brief: 1990년대 공장 마당에 쌓인 휴대폰 더미가 불타는 장면. 연기와 주황빛 불꽃, 멀리 작업복 차림 직원들의 실루엣. 실제 로고 없음.

head: Big, fast, cheap.
But not good.
body: In the early 1990s, Samsung was known for making a lot of electronics, not great ones. Factories chased volume targets.
In 1993, chairman Lee Kun-hee gathered executives in Frankfurt and told them to change everything about how they worked.

image.label: Executives in a hotel conference room in the early 1990s
image.brief: 1990년대 초 유럽 호텔 회의실에 모인 정장 차림 임원들의 뒷모습. 무거운 분위기. 얼굴은 보이지 않게.

head: A gift that
came back broken.
body: Samsung's Anycall phones were meant to take on Motorola, which led the Korean market. But quality lagged.
In a story often told, Lee gave phones as holiday gifts and heard back that many did not work.

image.label: A gift-wrapped phone box with a returned note
image.brief: 1990년대 한국 명절 선물 포장 상자 안의 휴대폰, 옆에 놓인 불만 메모. 따뜻한 실내 조명. 실제 상표 없음.

slides.label: phones and other devices pulled back, by most accounts
body: Samsung gathered up stock from the market and its warehouses. Reportedly it was worth about 50 billion won, a huge sum for a business still trying to win customers.

image.label: Warehouse shelves stacked with boxed phones
image.brief: 창고 선반에 가득 쌓인 휴대폰 상자들. 차가운 형광등. 브랜드 표시 없음.

head: A warehouse of bad phones.
What do you do?
body: You have tens of billions of won in faulty stock. Your workers think quality is someone else's job.

options.text: Fix the phones quietly and resell them at a discount
options.feedback: You recover some money. But the factory learns that defects can always be cleaned up later. Keep swiping.

options.text: Destroy all of them in front of the people who made them
options.feedback: You lose the stock for good, in public. The cost is the message. Keep swiping.

options.text: Add more inspectors at the end of the line
options.feedback: Fewer bad phones reach buyers, but the line still makes them. Keep swiping.

image.label: A factory manager facing stacks of returned devices
image.brief: 반품된 기기 더미 앞에 선 공장 관리자의 실루엣. 긴장된 공기, 1990년대 한국 공장.

head: A bonfire
at the factory.
body: In March 1995, at the Gumi plant, the devices were piled in a yard, smashed with hammers and set on fire.
Employees, many of whom had built them, stood and watched their own work burn.

image.label: Workers in uniforms watching a fire of phones
image.brief: 작업복을 입은 직원들이 줄지어 서서 불타는 기기 더미를 바라보는 뒷모습. 연기 사이로 공장 건물. 얼굴 식별 불가.

head: Quality stopped being
someone else's job.
body: The point was not the money. It was memory. Workers now knew a defect could cost everything they had made.
Samsung tightened its processes, and line workers reportedly gained the power to stop production when they found a problem.

image.label: A worker pressing a stop button on an assembly line
image.brief: 조립 라인에서 작업자의 손이 정지 버튼을 누르는 클로즈업. 1990년대 중반 공장.

head: From burned phones
to market leader.
body: Within a short time, Anycall was reported to have passed Motorola to lead the Korean phone market.
Samsung kept investing in quality and design, and in later decades became one of the world's largest phone makers.

image.label: A busy Seoul street with people using phones
image.brief: 1990년대 후반 서울 거리, 휴대폰으로 통화하는 사람들. 활기찬 도시 분위기. 실제 로고 없음.

head: Poor quality has a price.
Make everyone see it.
body: The cost of defects usually hides in returns, repairs and lost trust. Nobody on the line feels it.
Samsung turned that hidden cost into one public moment. A culture changes faster when people see what leaders will give up for a value.

image.label: Ashes on the ground with a single intact phone
image.brief: 재가 깔린 바닥 위에 멀쩡한 휴대폰 하나. 상징적인 정물 구도.

head: Values are proven
by what you give up.
body: Telling people quality matters rarely changes them. Showing them the real cost of getting it wrong does.
**Try it today:** pick one defect your team quietly fixes again and again. What would it look like to make its full cost visible to everyone?

image.label: A clean modern assembly line at dawn
image.brief: 새벽빛 속 깨끗하고 정돈된 현대식 조립 라인. 희망적인 톤.

factChecks.note: 화형식 날짜(1995년 3월 9일)와 장소(구미 사업장)는 삼성전자 사료와 당시 국내 언론 보도로 확인하세요. 카드에는 "In March 1995"와 "Gumi"로만 적었습니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] 1995년 3월 9일 구미 사업장 화형식 확인.

소각 물량 "약 15만 대"와 금액 "약 500억 원"은 널리 인용되는 수치지만, 휴대폰 외에 무선전화기·팩시밀리 등이 섞였다는 기록도 있습니다. 카드에는 "about"과 "reportedly"로 표시하고 "phones and other devices"로 적었습니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] 약 15만 대 확인. 금액은 500억 원(Korea Herald)과 150억 원(Korea Times)으로 엇갈려 'reportedly' 유지. 팩스·무선전화기 포함 보도도 있음.
이건희 회장이 설날 선물로 휴대폰을 돌렸다가 불량 불만을 들었다는 일화는 전해지는 이야기입니다. 카드에 "a story often told"로 표시했습니다.
1993년 프랑크푸르트 '신경영 선언'("마누라와 자식 빼고 다 바꿔라")은 널리 기록돼 있으나 직접 인용하지 않고 풀어서 썼습니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] 1993년 6월 프랑크푸르트 신경영 선언 확인.
애니콜이 1995년 무렵 국내 시장에서 모토로라를 제치고 1위에 올랐다는 내용은 당시 보도와 삼성 자료 기준입니다. 점유율 수치는 자료마다 달라 넣지 않았습니다.
직원 약 2,000명이 '품질 확보' 머리띠를 두르고 지켜봤다는 세부 묘사는 보도마다 차이가 있어 카드에는 "employees watched"로만 적었습니다.
